firmware/01-user-update-guide.title: Beginner guide: update a Tstat11
firmware/01-user-update-guide.html:
This is the normal, start-to-finish procedure for putting application firmware on a Tstat11 that already boots and communicates over RS485. It is intentionally different from the bootloader recovery procedure and from deploying a screen.

1. Choose the right operation#

Before changing anything, identify what you are trying to do:

Goal Do this Recompile firmware?
Change a touchscreen screen Deploy the screen JSON with Design Studio No
Correct a controller firmware problem Install temco_app.bin with T3000 Maybe—the binary may already exist
Recover or initialize the complete ESP32-S3 flash Use Flash Download Tool with the four-file bootloader package, then load temco_app.bin in T3000 Recovery files required

A Tstat11 has an existing bootloader when it leaves the factory. Do not reinstall the bootloader or partition table for a normal update.

2. What you need for a normal update#

  • A Tstat11 controller
  • Stable 24 V AC or DC power for the controller
  • A USB-to-RS485 adapter
  • T3000 software
  • The approved controller application image named temco_app.bin
  • Continuous power and RS485 connection during the update

Download T3000 from the TEMCO software page.

The application package may also contain ota_data_initial.bin. T3000's normal RS485 update selects temco_app.bin only. The OTA-data file belongs to a complete flash layout; do not select it as the application firmware in T3000.

3. Choose firmware#

Use one of these sources, in this order of preference:

  1. Production-approved release — the preferred choice for a deployed device.
  2. Successful GitHub Actions firmware artifact — useful for testing a known development commit.
  3. A locally built build\temco_app.bin — useful when developing and testing a change.

A GitHub artifact is the latest automated build, not automatically a production release. Confirm the branch, commit, build result and Tstat11 compatibility before flashing it.

If using the firmware repository, the currently documented CI artifact is from branch CB-Tstate-11, commit fc13533, and GitHub Actions build #75. Open the successful build, download its firmware artifact, and extract temco_app.bin.

Do not use an arbitrary firmware image merely because its file name is temco_app.bin.

4. Record the device state#

Before updating:

  1. Power the Tstat11 normally.
  2. In T3000, scan for and select the device.
  3. Confirm that the product/model shown is Tstat11.
  4. Record the device serial number.
  5. Record the current firmware version.
  6. Record the configured RS485 address and communication settings.
  7. If the site relies on custom settings, export or otherwise back up the controller configuration using the site's normal procedure.

Stop if the displayed model does not match the device or firmware target.

5. Connect the device#

  1. Connect the USB-to-RS485 adapter to the computer.
  2. Connect its RS485 terminals to the Tstat11's RS485 terminals.
  3. Observe the adapter's polarity and the device's terminal markings; do not guess A/B polarity.
  4. Open Windows Device Manager and note the adapter's COM port.
  5. Keep the Tstat11 on its stable 24 V supply.
  6. Open T3000 and scan for the device.
  7. Select the Tstat11 in the device list.

If the device does not appear, solve the connection before attempting an update.

6. Install the application firmware#

  1. In T3000, select Tools → Load firmware for a single device.
  2. Select the COM port assigned to the USB-to-RS485 adapter.
  3. Select 115200 baud.
  4. Select the confirmed temco_app.bin file.
  5. Recheck that the selected online device is the intended Tstat11.
  6. Start the firmware load.
  7. Keep power and RS485 connected until T3000 reports completion and the controller has rebooted.

Do not start a second update, remove power, or disconnect the adapter merely because the screen becomes blank during the transfer or reboot.

The update protocol saves progress and supports resuming an interrupted RS485 transfer. That is a recovery feature, not a reason to interrupt the update intentionally.

7. Verify the update#

After the device restarts:

  1. Scan again in T3000.
  2. Confirm that the same serial number appears.
  3. Confirm the expected firmware version or build identity.
  4. Check the display, I/O, RS485 communication and BACnet/Modbus access used by the installation.
  5. Check persistent schedules, network settings and other site-critical configuration.
  6. Run a short functional test appropriate to the site.

If the expected version is not visible, do not immediately flash a different bootloader. First confirm that the update completed, the correct firmware file was selected, and the intended device was addressed.

8. If the normal update fails#

Device is not found before the update#

  • Check 24 V power.
  • Check A/B polarity and the RS485 wiring.
  • Confirm the COM port in Device Manager.
  • Disconnect other software using the same COM port.
  • Confirm that the adapter is suitable for the network and baud rate.

Transfer is interrupted#

  • Restore power and the original RS485 connection if possible.
  • Restart T3000's single-device firmware loader with the same firmware file.
  • Use the tool's resume behavior where available.
  • Do not erase or directly program the flash during a recoverable transfer.

Device boots but behaves incorrectly#

  • Record the model, serial number, old version, new version and observed symptom.
  • Confirm that the image was intended for Tstat11.
  • Re-test with the known-good firmware selected for the site.
  • Contact the firmware owner before changing partition, signature or bootloader settings.

Device no longer boots or the boot/update environment is missing#

Use the Espressif Flash Download Tool procedure provided by the hardware developer. This is a full reflash, not the normal T3000 application update.

The approved package has two stages:

  1. Boot/update environment, from C:\Users\Double\Desktop\T3-S\Firmware\latest\bootloader:
    • bootloader.bin at 0x0
    • partition-table.bin at 0x8000
    • ota_data_initial.bin at 0x19000
    • T3_bootloader.bin at 0x20000
  2. Normal controller application, after reboot:
    • Load C:\Users\Double\Desktop\T3-S\Firmware\latest\ESP32\temco_app.bin with T3000.

These files are not interchangeable:

File Role
bootloader.bin ESP32-S3 first-stage bootloader
partition-table.bin Flash partition map
ota_data_initial.bin Initial OTA selection state
T3_bootloader.bin TEMCO factory application that performs later RS485 firmware updates
temco_app.bin Normal Tstat11 controller application

The four boot/update files come from the T3_Bootloader project's GitHub Actions build on branch Bhavik_Tstate11:

https://github.com/temcocontrols/T3_Bootloader/actions/workflows/build.yml

temco_app.bin comes from T3-programmable-controller-on-ESP32. Downloading, verifying and building each set is described in the developer guide. Actions artifacts expire, so keep the verified binaries you were given rather than relying on an old run link.

The Flash Download Tool is configured at:

Text
C:\Users\Double\Desktop\T3-S\flash_download_tool\flash_download_tool

Run the exact hardware connection/download-mode instructions for the Tstat11 board revision. The current saved tool configuration selects the four boot/update files and the addresses above. After those four files verify successfully, return to the normal T3000 procedure and load temco_app.bin over RS485.

Do not use temco_app.bin in place of T3_bootloader.bin, do not load both identically named concepts from an arbitrary directory, and do not reuse T3-Nano or TSTAT10 jumper instructions without hardware confirmation.

9. Completion checklist#

  • [ ] Correct Tstat11 model and serial number confirmed
  • [ ] Firmware source, branch/commit or release identified
  • [ ] Current version and configuration recorded
  • [ ] Correct temco_app.bin selected for a normal update
  • [ ] Power and RS485 remained connected during transfer
  • [ ] Device rebooted and was discovered again
  • [ ] Expected version and basic operation verified
  • [ ] Site-critical settings and communications verified

For source builds, continue with Developer guide: build and validate firmware. For protocol and recovery internals, see How a firmware update runs.

firmware/02-developer-build-guide.title: Developer guide: build and validate firmware
firmware/02-developer-build-guide.html:
This guide covers the development path from a clean checkout to a verified temco_app.bin. It is for firmware developers and release testers. A deployed Tstat11 should normally be updated with T3000 as described in the beginner update guide.

1. The two firmware projects#

Two separate ESP-IDF projects produce the files that end up on a Tstat11:

Project Builds Flashed by Lands in
T3_Bootloader bootloader.bin, partition-table.bin, ota_data_initial.bin, T3_bootloader.bin Flash Download Tool over UART 0x0, 0x8000, 0x19000, 0x20000
T3-programmable-controller-on-ESP32 temco_app.bin (plus its own bootloader.bin, partition-table.bin, ota_data_initial.bin) T3000 over RS485 OTA application partition

The name T3_bootloader.bin is easy to misunderstand. It is the ESP-IDF project output named T3_bootloader; it is an application binary placed in the 1 MB factory partition. It is not the same file as ESP-IDF's small bootloader.bin, which runs first at chip reset.

How the two projects relate#

File Produced by Same file?
bootloader.bin both projects No. Each project generates its own ESP-IDF stage-1 bootloader for its own sdkconfig.
partition-table.bin both projects No, and this matters. The two checked-in partition files currently disagree (see section 5).
ota_data_initial.bin both projects Yes, in the package examined here — both are 8192 bytes of identical content (ota_data_initial is "no OTA selection yet").
T3_bootloader.bin T3_Bootloader Only this project produces it.
temco_app.bin T3-programmable-controller-on-ESP32 Only this project produces it.

Consequences to keep in mind:

  • A normal application build does not rebuild the TEMCO bootloader/update application.
  • Building T3_Bootloader does not produce the current controller UI, protocol or I/O code.
  • Flashing the application project's own bootloader.bin or partition-table.bin over a working device is an unplanned layout change, not an application update.
  • temco_app.bin must fit the ota_0 partition defined by the installed partition table — not by whatever the application checkout happens to contain.

The documentation repositories are deliberately outside this firmware guide. The repository T3_Bootloader has no build guide of its own — its README.md is a one-line description, and its other documents cover the update protocol (FIRMWARE_UPDATE_FLOWCHART.md) and signing (File/Sign_Guide.md, File/Skip_Sign_Validation.md). The build and flash instructions live here, in this manual.

Which branch of T3_Bootloader builds the ESP32-S3 binaries#

Verified from the repository's branches:

Branch Target Flash Partition file ESP32-S3 boot/update set
main (the local checkout at C:\QN\temcocontrols\T3_Bootloader) esp32 4 MB, DIO temco_partitions.cvs, factory 0x10000, ota_0 0x110000 No
Bhavik_Tstate11 esp32s3 32 MB, OPI temco_partitions.csv, factory 0x20000 (1 MB), ota_0 0x120000 (6 MB), screen_data 0x780000 Yes
ResumableFirmwareUpdateBootloader esp32s3 32 MB temco_partitions.csv Yes — earlier line, merged into Bhavik_Tstate11
SecureFirmwareUpdate esp32 4 MB temco_partitions.cvs No

So the local checkout as configured on main cannot produce the packaged ESP32-S3 files. Its partition table has different offsets, and its sdkconfig targets ESP32 with 4 MB flash.

Bhavik_Tstate11 also carries code that main does not: main/wifi_web_server.c, main/LCD_Driver/, and an idf_component.yml requiring espressif/mdns.

To build the ESP32-S3 set locally:

PowerShell
Set-Location "C:\QN\temcocontrols\T3_Bootloader"
git status                   # must be clean before switching
git fetch origin
git switch --track origin/Bhavik_Tstate11
git log -1 --oneline

Confirm the checked-in configuration before compiling:

PowerShell
Select-String -Path .\sdkconfig -Pattern '^CONFIG_IDF_TARGET=|^CONFIG_ESPTOOLPY_FLASHSIZE=|^CONFIG_PARTITION_TABLE_CUSTOM_FILENAME='
# expect: esp32s3 / 32MB / temco_partitions.csv

From an ESP-IDF 5.5 PowerShell terminal:

PowerShell
idf.py --version    # must report 5.5.3
idf.py fullclean
idf.py build

To reproduce the packaged set exactly rather than the newest code:

PowerShell
git switch --detach 95d60a06
idf.py fullclean
idf.py build

Expected outputs:

Text
build\bootloader\bootloader.bin            ~21 KB
build\partition_table\partition-table.bin   3072 B
build\ota_data_initial.bin                  8192 B
build\T3_bootloader.bin                     ~840 KB   (must stay under 1 MB)

Rules for this build:

  • Do not run idf.py set-target esp32s3. The committed sdkconfig is already esp32s3; set-target regenerates it from defaults, renames the existing file to sdkconfig.old, and drops this project's settings.
  • The first build downloads espressif/mdns from the component registry — network access is required. dependencies.lock pins version 1.13.1.
  • No temco_bacnet / temco_IO_control copy is needed here. That step belongs to the application project only.
  • Switching branches rewrites sdkconfig and removes temco_partitions.cvs. Switch back to main when you need the ESP32 line.

Verify the result before flashing:

PowerShell
& 'C:\Espressif\python_env\idf5.5_py3.11_env\Scripts\esptool.exe' --chip esp32s3 image_info .\build\bootloader\bootloader.bin
& 'C:\Espressif\python_env\idf5.5_py3.11_env\Scripts\python.exe' `
  'C:\Espressif\frameworks\esp-idf-v5.5.3\components\partition_table\gen_esp32part.py' `
  .\build\partition_table\partition-table.bin

The decoded table must show factory at 0x20000 size 1M and ota_0 at 0x120000 size 6M. If it shows 0x10000 / 0x110000, the build came from main, not from Bhavik_Tstate11.

2. Prerequisites#

Install or obtain:

  • Git with submodule support
  • Espressif ESP-IDF 5.5.3 for source builds
  • The tools installed by the ESP-IDF Windows installer
  • T3000 and a USB-to-RS485 adapter for normal application updates
  • Espressif Flash Download Tool and the approved four-file bootloader package for full reflash/recovery
  • Optionally, ESP-IDF Eclipse if the IDE workflow is preferred

The working T3-S recovery tool is under C:\Users\Double\Desktop\T3-S\flash_download_tool\flash_download_tool. Do not confuse this low-level UART tool with T3000's RS485 firmware loader.

Use installation and project paths without spaces. Open an ESP-IDF 5.5 PowerShell terminal so that idf.py and the toolchain are configured.

Confirm the environment:

PowerShell
idf.py --version
git --version

The version command must report ESP-IDF 5.5.3 or the explicitly approved maintenance build for the same toolchain line.

3. Select the source state#

Move to the firmware repository:

PowerShell
Set-Location "C:\QN\temcocontrols\T3-programmable-controller-on-ESP32"
git status
git branch --show-current
git rev-parse HEAD
git submodule update --init --recursive

For a Tstat11 change, use the branch assigned to that development line. The current Tstat11-focused source examined for this guide is CB-Tstate-11; do not silently build another product branch.

Before building a release candidate, record:

  • Branch
  • Exact commit SHA
  • Whether the tree is clean
  • ESP-IDF version
  • Target: esp32s3
  • Any local patches not present in the commit

A dirty tree must not be treated as a reproducible release build.

4. Integrate the modified ESP-IDF components#

The project contains TEMCO replacements for two components. The CI workflow copies them into the ESP-IDF component directory before building:

PowerShell
Copy-Item ".\temco_bacnet" "$env:IDF_PATH\components\temco_bacnet" -Recurse -Force
Copy-Item ".\temco_IO_control" "$env:IDF_PATH\components\temco_IO_control" -Recurse -Force

Use a dedicated ESP-IDF installation when possible because these commands replace files below IDF_PATH.

If using an IDE-created ESP-IDF installation, verify that $env:IDF_PATH points to the intended installation before copying.

5. Verify the build target and layout#

The checked-in configuration currently specifies:

  • CONFIG_IDF_TARGET=esp32s3
  • 32 MB flash
  • Custom partition table: temco_partitions.csv
  • Project/application name: temco_app

Review the partition table whenever changing flash-related code. The application and the installed bootloader must agree on the same partition names, offsets and sizes. Never copy an address list from an older product manual into a current build.

The current file is temco_partitions.csv. The generated build's flash_args and flasher_args.json are authoritative for that specific build.

The approved four-file Flash Download Tool package has a different layout: factory 0x20000 size 1 MB and ota_0 0x120000 size 6 MB. This is the layout decoded from its packaged partition-table.bin, and it is exactly the temco_partitions.csv on the bootloader branch Bhavik_Tstate11.

The application project's file is the other variant — the comments in it call it "for flash directly without bootloader": factory 0x20000 size 6 MB and ota_0 0x620000 size 1 MB.

This is not cosmetic. The application image is about 2.7 MB, so under the application project's layout it would not fit the 1 MB ota_0 partition at 0x620000, and an RS485 update would fail. Under the bootloader layout it fits comfortably in the 6 MB ota_0 at 0x120000.

Therefore: when testing an application build, the partition table that is actually on the device decides where the update lands. Do not flash the application project's partition-table.bin over the bootloader's.

6. Build from the command line#

From the firmware repository root:

PowerShell
idf.py build

For a clean reproducibility check:

PowerShell
Remove-Item .\build -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
idf.py build

Expected primary output:

Text
build\temco_app.bin

Expected supporting build data includes:

Text
build\flash_args
build\flasher_args.json
build\partition_table\partition-table.bin
build\bootloader\bootloader.bin

A successful build means that those files were produced, but it does not establish hardware compatibility.

7. Build with ESP-IDF Eclipse#

  1. Open ESP-IDF Eclipse.
  2. Select File → Import.
  3. Select Espressif → Existing IDF Project.
  4. Select the firmware repository root.
  5. Confirm the target is ESP32-S3 and the ESP-IDF version is 5.5.3.
  6. Right-click the project and select Build Project.
  7. Inspect build\temco_app.bin and the generated flash arguments.

Use the command-line build in automation and for final reproducibility checks.

8. Build with GitHub Actions#

Both projects build in GitHub Actions. The artifacts are the intended way to obtain binaries without a local toolchain — but they expire, and each project publishes a different, non-interchangeable set.

8.1 The bootloader project#

Workflow: .github/workflows/build.yml in temcocontrols/T3_Bootloader.

It runs espressif/idf:v5.5.3, executes idf.py fullclean then idf.py build, and uploads one artifact named firmware containing:

Text
build/bootloader/bootloader.bin
build/partition_table/partition-table.bin
build/*.bin        ← includes ota_data_initial.bin and T3_bootloader.bin

Only pushes to Bhavik_Tstate11 produce the ESP32-S3 set. Building main in Actions yields the ESP32/4 MB set.

Download through the browser

  1. Open https://github.com/temcocontrols/T3_Bootloader/actions/workflows/build.yml.
  2. Use the branch filter and select Bhavik_Tstate11.
  3. Open the run you want (the newest successful one, or the specific commit).
  4. Confirm the run's conclusion is ✔ and note the branch and commit SHA.
  5. In the run summary page, scroll to Artifacts and click firmware.
  6. The browser downloads firmware.zip. Extract it; it contains the binaries (sometimes as an inner firmware.zip with the same name, which must be extracted too).
  7. Record the SHA-256 of each file before flashing.

Signing in to GitHub is required; artifacts from a private repository are not anonymous downloads, and each artifact expires (the retention window is shown on the artifact row — the run examined here expires 2026-12-06 and 2026-12-30 respectively).

Download with the GitHub CLI

PowerShell
gh run list --repo temcocontrols/T3_Bootloader --branch Bhavik_Tstate11 --limit 10
gh run download <run-id> --repo temcocontrols/T3_Bootloader --name firmware --dir .\bootloader-pack

Download with the REST API

The artifact ZIP requires an authenticated request:

PowerShell
$headers = @{ Authorization = "Bearer $env:GITHUB_TOKEN" }
Invoke-WebRequest -Headers $headers -OutFile .\firmware.zip `
  'https://api.github.com/repos/temcocontrols/T3_Bootloader/actions/artifacts/<artifact-id>/zip'

8.2 The application project#

Workflow: .github/workflows/build.yml in temcocontrols/T3-programmable-controller-on-ESP32.

It runs an ESP-IDF 5.5.3 container, copies temco_bacnet and temco_IO_control into the IDF components directory, executes idf.py build, and uploads build/*.bin as a firmware artifact. That artifact includes temco_app.bin and the application project's own bootloader.bin, partition-table.bin and ota_data_initial.bin.

Download it the same way, from:

https://github.com/temcocontrols/T3-programmable-controller-on-ESP32/actions/workflows/build.yml

For an application artifact:

  1. Open the workflow run for the exact commit.
  2. Confirm the workflow conclusion is successful.
  3. Confirm the branch and full commit SHA.
  4. Download the firmware artifact.
  5. Take temco_app.bin for T3000. Do not flash the application project's bootloader.bin or partition-table.bin as part of a normal update.
  6. Record or calculate a SHA-256 checksum before transfer.

A newer timestamp alone is not enough to classify a build as a release.

8.3 Provenance of the packaged latest bootloader files#

The package under C:\Users\Double\Desktop\T3-S\Firmware\latest\bootloader corresponds to an Actions build, not to the local main checkout:

Fact Value
Workflow Build Firmware #47
Branch Bhavik_Tstate11
Commit 95d60a06f785a51388114e9365718d120994db36 — "Updated partition to store Dynamic screen data"
Run https://github.com/temcocontrols/T3_Bootloader/actions/runs/34086246535
Artifact firmware, id 10005379381, created 2026-09-07 05:21:55 UTC
Evidence the artifact creation time matches the local file timestamps (2026-09-07), and the decoded partition table matches commit 95d60a06
Artifact expiry 2026-12-06

Two later successful builds exist on the same branch — #48 (8ae3b79, Modbus/UART fixes), #49 (c2f7fbd, Wi-Fi SoftAP + web server) and #50 (9329f55, lint) — so the packaged set is older than the newest bootloader code. Do not assume "latest" in the folder name means the newest commit.

9. Run checks before hardware installation#

Run the repository's host unit tests according to Testing the firmware without hardware.

Also review:

  • Build completed without errors
  • No unexpected warnings in the changed area
  • temco_app.bin fits the application partition
  • Partition definitions match the target device
  • Firmware version/build identity is visible or traceable to the commit
  • Required custom components were included
  • No private key, credential or machine-specific path is in the output

For a security-sensitive or production image, validate the approved signing process before deployment.

10. The two installation flows#

A. Normal application update — use T3000#

Use this when the controller boots and the TEMCO bootloader/update application is present:

  1. Connect power and USB-to-RS485.
  2. Scan and select the exact Tstat11.
  3. Open Tools → Load firmware for a single device.
  4. Select the COM port, 115200 baud, and temco_app.bin from T3-programmable-controller-on-ESP32.
  5. Keep power connected through completion and reboot.

T3000 sends temco_app.bin through the bootloader's RS485 update protocol. The updater validates the transfer and places the main application in the OTA application slot. The ota_data_initial.bin from an application build is metadata for a complete direct flash; it is not selected as a firmware file in T3000.

B. Full reflash — use Espressif Flash Download Tool#

Use this when instructed to recover or initialize the complete ESP32-S3 flash environment. The saved T3-S tool configuration at:

Text
C:\Users\Double\Desktop\T3-S\flash_download_tool\flash_download_tool

uses the following four-file package:

File Address Meaning
bootloader.bin 0x0 ESP32-S3 first-stage bootloader
partition-table.bin 0x8000 Partition names, addresses and sizes
ota_data_initial.bin 0x19000 Initial OTA-selection state
T3_bootloader.bin 0x20000 TEMCO factory application that handles firmware updates

The latest package checked for this guide is:

Text
C:\Users\Double\Desktop\T3-S\Firmware\latest\bootloader\

Its partition table decodes to a 1 MB factory partition at 0x20000, a 6 MB ota_0 application partition at 0x120000, and the remaining data partitions. The configured first-stage file starts with an ESP32-S3 image header.

After the four-file flash succeeds, the device has the boot/update environment, but the full controller application still must be installed. Return to T3000 and transfer the approved temco_app.bin. Do not select an arbitrary file named ota_data_initial.bin for this second step; the two packages contain identical OTA data, but T3000's normal application transfer uses temco_app.bin only.

11. Full-reflash procedure#

  1. Confirm with the hardware owner that the ESP32-S3 is in UART download mode and that the correct programming connector/power arrangement is used.
  2. Start flash_download_tool_3.9.9_R2.exe from the T3-S flash tool folder.
  3. Choose the ESP32-S3 download target and UART mode.
  4. Select and verify these four rows:
Text
C:\Users\Double\Desktop\T3-S\Firmware\latest\bootloader\bootloader.bin       @ 0x0
C:\Users\Double\Desktop\T3-S\Firmware\latest\bootloader\partition-table.bin  @ 0x8000
C:\Users\Double\Desktop\T3-S\Firmware\latest\bootloader\ota_data_initial.bin @ 0x19000
C:\Users\Double\Desktop\T3-S\Firmware\latest\bootloader\T3_bootloader.bin    @ 0x20000
  1. Select the correct COM port. The saved example uses COM5, but the local port must be confirmed in Device Manager.
  2. Erase/download using the hardware developer's approved settings and wait for all four rows to verify successfully.
  3. Remove download mode and reboot as instructed for the board.
  4. Confirm the device identifies itself as the bootloader/update environment.
  5. Use T3000 over RS485 to load temco_app.bin from the approved application package.
  6. Reboot and run the hardware validation checklist.

Do not substitute files from the other flow, do not shift these addresses, and do not flash only T3_bootloader.bin as though it were bootloader.bin.

Source and package warning — now confirmed#

The local checkout C:\QN\temcocontrols\T3_Bootloader is the source repository for the TEMCO bootloader/update project, but it is on main, which targets ESP32 / 4 MB with temco_partitions.cvs. The packaged latest binaries are ESP32-S3 and use the 32 MB layout above.

Confirmed: the correct source is branch Bhavik_Tstate11, and the packaged files come from Build Firmware #47 (commit 95d60a06) — see section 8.3.

Do not rebuild or replace the four-file package from the local main checkout: the resulting partition-table.bin and bootloader.bin would not match the addresses the flash tool uses or the layout temco_app.bin expects. Switch to Bhavik_Tstate11 first, or download the artifact from the matching run.

12. Hardware validation checklist#

After reboot, verify at least:

  • [ ] Device is rediscovered in T3000 with the expected serial number
  • [ ] Expected firmware version/build is reported
  • [ ] Touchscreen and home screen start normally
  • [ ] 24 V power interruption/restart behaves normally
  • [ ] Network configuration persists
  • [ ] RS485 Modbus operates
  • [ ] BACnet path required by the change operates
  • [ ] Sensor/input values are plausible
  • [ ] Output control behaves safely in the intended test setup
  • [ ] Dynamic display screen loading still operates
  • [ ] Schedules and persisted settings survive reboot
  • [ ] No repeated boot, watchdog or allocation failures appear

Attach test evidence—commit SHA, binary checksum, tester, date, device serial number and results—to the release or change record.

13. Recommended release identity#

For a development or production build, preserve a package record containing:

Text
Product: Tstat11
Firmware file: temco_app.bin
Branch: <branch>
Commit: <40-character SHA>
ESP-IDF: 5.5.3
ESP target: esp32s3
Build date: <UTC date/time>
SHA-256: <digest>
CI run: <URL or local build>
Test device: <serial/model/revision>
Signature status: <signed/unsigned/not-applicable>
Approval: <development/test/production>

Do not publish a CI artifact as the latest product firmware without release approval.

14. Failure boundaries#

Stop and investigate rather than forcing a flash when:

  • The product/model cannot be confirmed.
  • The bootloader or partition layout differs from the selected firmware.
  • The image comes from an unrelated branch.
  • T3000 targets a different serial device.
  • The firmware requires a signing setting that is not understood.
  • The update instructions combine T3-Nano, TSTAT10 and Tstat11 hardware details.

The normal application update is intentionally the simplest route. The harder build, signing, partition and direct-flash details are development and recovery tools, not required beginner steps.

firmware/building.title: Building the firmware
firmware/building.html:
ESP-IDF 5.5.3, two components moved into the IDF tree, and an Eclipse project that is imported rather than generated. The path matters: the IDF installer cannot cope with a path that contains spaces.

Start here: Use the developer guide for the complete, reproducible workflow and the beginner guide when the goal is only to install an existing application image on a Tstat11.

Compiling#

ESP32 code#

Please download the ESP idf integrated development environment from Espressif to compile the code, the version is 5.5.3.

1. Install the ESP-IDF tool installer

Go to the https://github.com/espressif/idf-installer/releases/download/offline-5.5.3/esp-idf-tools-setup-offline-5.5.3.exe

page where you can download the esp - idf - tools - setup. The IDE should be installed in a path that does not contain spaces in the name.

2. Run esp-idf-tools-setup-offline-5.5.3.exe

You can change the default ESP IDF installation path, which will be used later.

3. Once installed, you should get an ESP-IDF Eclipse, which is the compiler we used to compile ESP32 code.

4. Move the two folders, temco_bacnet and temco_IO_control, from the code download on Github to the components directory in esp-idf, replacing the original driver folder. This is the change we made to the IDF.

5. Open the ESP-IDF Eclipse program, File ->Import, Espressif ->Existing IDF Project, select the project directory downloaded from github, and click Finish to load the project into the compiler.

6. Right click the project name and select Build Project to compile. This will take a while the first time.

7. Once the compile is complete, you will see the 'temco_app.bin' file in the 'build' directory within your imported project.

6. You can get more help from

https://esp32.com/index.php
https://espressif-docs.readthedocs-hosted.com/projects/esp-idf/en/latest/index.html

T3-NANO's STM32 code#

Typically, Keil V5 ARM is used to compile and generate firmware. The project file is located at \T3-nano-stm\MDK-ARM Much of the code is generated using the STM32CubeMX software.

firmware/flashing.title: Loading firmware onto a device
firmware/flashing.html:
Normally the bootloader is already in the product when it ships, and a firmware update goes through T3000 over RS485. Use the beginner guide for the complete normal Tstat11 workflow.

For the current T3-S/Tstat11 full-reflash flow, use the confirmed four-file Flash Download Tool package and address map documented in the beginner guide and developer guide. The four-file stage installs the first-stage bootloader, partition table, OTA data and T3_bootloader.bin; T3000 then installs the normal temco_app.bin over RS485.

The T3-Nano and TSTAT10 procedures below are retained as legacy hardware reference. Their headers, jumpers and download sequences must not be mixed into the Tstat11 procedure.

In general, there is no need to personally load the Bootloader firmware to the product, it is already done before the factory. In special cases, follow the steps below to reload the Bootloader firmware.

Update the main firmware#

Download T3000 software,https://assets.temcocontrols.com/products/t3_series_programmable_bacnet__amp_modbus_controller/software_file/09T3000Software-4.zip. Connect the device to PC with RS485, open T3000, click the icon to search for the device, if the connection is normal, the device will appear in the list. Select the device you want to update and click Tools->Load firmware for a single device to start the update.

Load the bootloader firmware to T3-nano#

1. Software tools and firmware

  • ESP32 download firmware tool and ESP32 firmware https://temcocontrols.com/ftp/file/flash_download_tool_v3.8.5.zip https://temcocontrols.com/ftp/file/BootloaderT3NanoRev27.zip
  • CH340SerSetup for USB-to-TTL debug board https://temcocontrols.com/ftp/file/CH340SerSetup.zip
  • UartAssist.exe print debug messages via USB-to-TTL board https://temcocontrols.com/ftp/file/UartAssist.zip

2. Print Debugging Information

  • Plug USB-to-TTL debug board to your PC , Download and install CH341 driver , you will find a new USB-SERIAL CH340(COMXX) under device manager->Ports .
  • Connect the USB-to-TTL debugging board and motherboard J4 through the male and female connector , pay attention to keep MARK point in the same position .
  • Power on and open commUart Assistant which print some messages about sensors.

3. ESP32 update firmware .

  • Hardware connection USB-to-TTL connect to J3 , Short J5 and J6 by a jumper until the end of the download firmware , turn on 24V power .
  • Set ESP32 firmware download tool configurations. Run flash_download_tool_3.8.5.exe , Tools -> Developer Mode -> ESP32 Download Tool, Set some options as shown .


    ESP32 firmware contains four parts

  • Click the Start button to download the latest firmware . When it show Finish , please remove jumper on J5 & J6 and power on again, If UartAssist.exe is running , you can see debugging messages .

Load the bootloader firmware to TSTAT10#

1. Connect TSTAT10 J3 to USB with a USB to TTL debug board


Jumper J1, so that after restarting, it will enter flash download mode, momentarily jumper J2, and TSTAT10 will restart and prepare to download the bootloader. USB to TTL dongle has a 3.3V power supply, and if power supply is insufficient, you can connect 24V power to the TSTAT10.

2. The steps to use the ESP32 flash downloader software are the same as the T3-nano.

3. Keep in mind that the ESP32 flash downloader tool is only used to install the bootloaders and partition information.

4. On a TSTAT10 with its RS485 port, a USB to RS485 adapter can be used by the flash download tool embedded within the T3000 software

Power the TSTat10 with 24V AC or DC Connect the USB to RS485 adapter to your computer and the jack on the TSTAT10. Launch the T3000 software and select Tools -> Load firmware to a single device Then select the com port of your adapter, the baud rate as 115200 and the temco_app.bin file from your build path Press the flash button and the device will be programmed with your binary before rebooting to launch

firmware/mqtt-guide.title: MQTT publishing
firmware/mqtt-guide.html:
A controller can publish its points to a broker, so a dashboard or a historian does not have to poll it. This page is the operator side: the control register that turns it on, the broker it expects, and how to watch the topics with MQTTX.

This guide provides instructions on how to enable, configure, and monitor MQTT communication on the T3 ESP32 Programmable Controller. It also details how to use MQTTX to verify connection status and monitor data transmission.

1. MQTT Overview#

The T3 ESP32 controller integrates a lightweight MQTT client that connects to the public HiveMQ broker to publish real-time point changes via Change of Value (COV) notifications. This allows integration with cloud platforms, SCADA systems, or custom IoT dashboards.

2. Modbus Configuration Details#

To manage the MQTT service on the T3 controller, you must read or write to specific Modbus register values. The configuration details are as follows:

MQTT Control Register#

Modbus Register (0-Indexed) Modbus Address (1-Indexed) Description Data Type Permitted Values Default
24 25 Enable/Disable MQTT Service Unsigned 8-bit 0 = Disabled
1 = Enabled		 0 (Disabled)

[!NOTE] Modbus register changes are automatically saved to the controller's non-volatile storage (NVS) flash partition. This ensures the setting persists across device reboots and power cycles.

Hardcoded Broker Specifications#

Currently, the broker information is hardcoded in the device firmware to facilitate plug-and-play testing:

  • Broker Address/Host: broker.hivemq.com
  • Port: 1883 (Standard unencrypted TCP port)
  • Protocol: mqtt:// (Standard MQTT over TCP)
  • Encryption/Credentials: None required (Public testing broker)

[!WARNING] Since the HiveMQ public broker (broker.hivemq.com) is a shared, unencrypted public server, it should not be used for sensitive production deployments.

3. Network Prerequisites#

For the MQTT client to initiate a connection, the following prerequisites must be met:

  1. The controller must have a valid network connection (Ethernet or Wi-Fi).
  2. The controller must obtain an IP address.
  3. Modbus Register 24 must be written with a value of 1.

On startup, the MQTT handler task will block and print Waiting for WiFi connection... until the network connection is established, after which it will start the MQTT client and connect.

4. Monitoring MQTT Data with MQTTX#

MQTTX is a cross-platform MQTT client tool designed for developers to test MQTT connections, publish, and subscribe to topics.

A. Downloading and Installing MQTTX#

  1. Visit the official website: https://mqttx.app/.
  2. Click on the Download button.
  3. Choose the installer appropriate for your Operating System:
    • Windows: .exe installer or portable version.
    • macOS: .dmg installer (Intel or Apple Silicon).
    • Linux: .AppImage or .deb package.
  4. Run the installer and follow the wizard instructions to complete installation.

B. Configuring a New Connection in MQTTX#

  1. Open the MQTTX application.
  2. Click the + New Connection button in the left sidebar or the center of the window.
  3. Configure the connection settings as follows:
    • Name: T3 ESP32 Controller (or any descriptive name)
    • Client ID: Leave as default (randomly generated)
    • Host: mqtt://broker.hivemq.com
    • Port: 1883
    • Username / Password: Leave blank (no credentials required)
    • SSL/TLS: Disabled
    • MQTT Version: 3.1.1 (or 5.0)
  4. Click the Connect button in the top right corner. The connection status circle should turn green and show Connected.

C. Subscribing to T3 Controller Topics#

Once connected to the broker, you can subscribe to topics to receive messages published by the controller.

  1. Click the + New Subscription button.
  2. Configure the subscription:
    • Topic: temco/cov/tstat11/#
    • QoS: 1
  3. Click Confirm.

[!IMPORTANT] Active BACnet Subscription Requirement: By default, the controller operates in BACnet Subscription COV mode. In this mode, the controller will only publish COV messages to MQTT for objects that have an active BACnet subscription registered from a BACnet client/workstation (such as Yabe). If no BACnet client is actively subscribed to a point, the controller will not publish its updates to the MQTT broker.

  • To verify and trigger data, connect to the controller using a BACnet tool and subscribe to the Change-of-Value (COV) properties for the objects you want to monitor.
  • If you want all values to publish automatically without requiring a BACnet subscription, the device firmware configuration must be compiled with ALL_COV enabled.

[!TIP] The wildcard # in temco/cov/tstat11/# allows you to receive notifications for all objects on all devices. If you only want to monitor a specific device or object type, use a specific topic (see Topic Structure below).

D. MQTT Topic Structure and Payload#

The controller publishes COV events using JSON format.

1. Device Diagnostics & Connection Handshake Topic

Upon a successful connection to the HiveMQ broker, the controller publishes a hello message to confirm its status:

  • Topic: temco/test/tstat11/pub
  • Payload Example:
    JSON
    {
  "status": "online",
  "device": "tstat11",
  "device_id":"1028",
  "broker": "HiveMQ"
}

2. COV Notification Topic

When a point's value changes, the controller publishes to a topic structured by its device instance and object type:

  • Topic Format: temco/cov/tstat11/device_<Device_ID>/<Object_Type>_<Instance>
    • <Device_ID>: The unique BACnet device instance number (e.g., 12345).
    • <Object_Type>: The object type name (e.g., ANALOG_INPUT, BINARY_VALUE, etc.).
    • <Instance>: The 1-based index of the object (e.g., 1 for Input 1).
  • Example Topic: temco/cov/tstat11/device_12345/ANALOG_INPUT_1
  • Payload Example:
    JSON
    {
  "subscriber_process_id": 1,
  "initiating_device_id": 12345,
  "time_remaining": 60,
  "monitored_object": {
    "type": 0,
    "type_name": "ANALOG_INPUT",
    "instance": 1
  },
  "values": [
    {
      "property_id": 85,
      "property_name": "PRESENT_VALUE",
      "property_array_index": 4294967295,
      "priority": 16,
      "tag": 4,
      "value": 23.5
    }
  ]
}

E. Initiating Point Subscriptions via MQTT

If you do not want to use a BACnet tool to subscribe to points, you can initiate subscriptions directly via MQTT by publishing a subscription control JSON payload.

The controller listens for subscription messages on the following topics:

  • temco/test/tstat11/sub
  • temco/cov/tstat11/sub
1. JSON Subscription Request Format

Publish a JSON message containing the target point details:

JSON
{
  "action": "subscribe",
  "object_type": "ANALOG_INPUT",
  "instance": 1,
  "lifetime": 300
}
  • action: Must be "subscribe".
  • object_type: The BACnet object type. Can be numeric (e.g. 0 for Analog Input) or a string:
    • 0 or "ANALOG_INPUT"
    • 1 or "ANALOG_OUTPUT"
    • 2 or "ANALOG_VALUE"
    • 3 or "BINARY_INPUT"
    • 4 or "BINARY_OUTPUT"
    • 5 or "BINARY_VALUE"
  • instance: The 1-based point number (e.g. 1 for Input 1).
  • lifetime: (Optional) Remaining time in seconds before subscription expires. Defaults to 300 (5 minutes) if omitted.
2. JSON Unsubscribe Request Format

To cancel a subscription before it expires, publish an unsubscribe message:

JSON
{
  "action": "unsubscribe",
  "object_type": "ANALOG_INPUT",
  "instance": 1
}
3. Unified BACnet Integration Scheme

The controller manages MQTT subscriptions by forwarding them directly to the native BACnet stack's COV engine. This design:

  1. Supports All 6 Point Types Natively: It registers and tracks Analog Input, Analog Output, Analog Value, Binary Input, Binary Output, and Binary Value (types 0 to 5) uniformly through the local BACnet stack.
  2. Fully Event-Driven: It avoids redundant background loops and polling code inside the MQTT client task. When a point changes, the BACnet stack immediately triggers a callback to package and publish the new value to MQTT.
  3. No Extra Memory Overhead: It eliminates the need for duplicate comparison tables, custom flash storage (NVS) arrays, or excessive CPU cycles, keeping the firmware lightweight and optimized for the ESP32-S3 platform.
  4. No Local Network Traffic: Since the subscription is processed locally, it does not send requests over the physical network interface; instead, it registers them directly within the local COV subsystem.

This guarantees that subscribing via MQTT works seamlessly and efficiently for all 6 object types.

5. Troubleshooting Checklist#

  • No Messages Received in MQTTX:
    1. Verify that Modbus Register 24 is set to 1 (use a Modbus poll tool like Modscan/Yabe to confirm).
    2. Check that the controller is connected to the same network and has internet access (required to reach broker.hivemq.com).
    3. Verify your Wi-Fi or Ethernet settings.
    4. Verify you are subscribed to the correct topic pattern in MQTTX (temco/cov/tstat11/#).
    5. Verify that either a BACnet client has subscribed to the COV, or you have successfully published a subscription JSON request to temco/cov/tstat11/sub.
    6. Enable verbose MQTT debugging prints on the ESP32 console by defining #define MQTT_DEBUG_EN 1 at the top of Mqtt_Handler.c. Recompile and flash the firmware, then monitor the serial output to trace subscription parsing and forwarding results.
  • Client disconnects or shows TCP errors:
    1. The public HiveMQ broker may be experiencing high load or temporary downtime. Try pinging broker.hivemq.com from a PC connected to the same network to check connectivity.

firmware/mqtt-implementation.title: How the MQTT task works
firmware/mqtt-implementation.html:
Three ways a change of value can reach the broker, how a point’s type becomes a JSON value, and how the topic name is assembled. Read this when the topic is arriving but the payload is not what a subscriber expected.

This document provides a technical overview of the MQTT client implementation on the T3 ESP32 Programmable Controller (ESP32-S3 platform). It outlines the architecture, initialization lifecycle, and details the two primary Change-of-Value (COV) paradigms supported by the system.

1. Architectural Overview#

The MQTT integration is located in the Mqtt_Handler folder, consisting of:

  • Mqtt_Handler.h: Public APIs, constants, and preprocessor configuration switches.
  • Mqtt_Handler.c: Task initialization, event loop handling, payload serialization (JSON), and polling/filtering routines.

Key Dependencies#

  • ESP-IDF v5 MQTT Client (esp-mqtt): Handles transport, TCP connection, TLS (optional), handshakes, and packet retries.
  • cJSON: Used for dynamic serialization of BACnet COV data into JSON strings.
  • BACnet Protocol Stack: Integrates with BACnet object types, properties, and values.

2. Initialization & Lifecycle Management#

The MQTT client lifecycle is tightly coupled with the controller's main task scheduler and Modbus registers.

MERMAID
flowchart TD
    A[Modbus Register 24 Written] --> B{Value == 1?}
    B -- Yes --> C[Mqtt_Handler_Init]
    B -- No --> D[Mqtt_Deinit]
    C --> E{Task already running?}
    E -- No --> F[xTaskCreate Mqtt_HandlerTask]
    F --> G[Wait for WIFI_CONNECTED_BIT]
    G --> H[esp_mqtt_client_init & Start]
    H --> I[Connect to broker.hivemq.com]
    D --> J[Set mqtt_task_exit = true]
    J --> K[esp_mqtt_client_stop & Destroy]
    K --> L[Delete Task]

A. Task Spawning (Mqtt_Handler_Init)#

The function Mqtt_Handler_Init() is called during system startup or when a write operation occurs on Modbus Register 24 (MODBUS_ENABLE_MQTT):

C
void Mqtt_Handler_Init(void)
{
    if(Modbus.enable_mqtt)
    {
        if (main_task_handle[19] != NULL) return; // Prevent duplicate tasks
        mqtt_task_exit = false;
        xTaskCreate(Mqtt_HandlerTask, "mqtt_handler", 4096, NULL, tskIDLE_PRIORITY + 2, &main_task_handle[19]);
    }
}

B. Task De-initialization (Mqtt_Deinit)#

When Modbus Register 24 is written with 0, Mqtt_Deinit() sets mqtt_task_exit = true. The task loops terminates, unregisters event handlers, stops the MQTT client, destroys the client handle, and deletes itself.

3. The Event Loop and Connection Handshake#

Inside Mqtt_HandlerTask, execution is blocked until Wi-Fi reports connection status:

  1. Wi-Fi Check: Blocks on s_wifi_event_group until WIFI_CONNECTED_BIT is set.
  2. Configuration: Configures the client with standard unencrypted TCP:
    C
    esp_mqtt_client_config_t mqtt_cfg = {
    .broker = {
        .address.uri = "mqtt://broker.hivemq.com:1883",
    },
};
  3. Event Registration: Registers mqtt_event_handler for connection updates, publishing failures, subscriptions, and TCP/TLS socket transport diagnostics.
  4. Handshake Pub/Sub:
    • Subscribes to: temco/test/tstat11/sub (QoS 1)
    • Publishes to: temco/test/tstat11/pub with connection payload {"status":"online","device":"tstat11","broker":"HiveMQ"}.

4. Change-of-Value (COV) Execution Paradigms#

The codebase supports two distinct mechanisms for detecting and dispatching data changes over MQTT. These are configured via macros in Mqtt_Handler.h.

Mechanism A: "All COV" Mode (ALL_COV)#

Note: This mode has been retired and disabled to optimize CPU cycles and minimize RAM usage by removing large global backup arrays (which would occupy over 1.5KB of memory).

Mechanism B: BACnet Subscription COV Mode (BACNET_SUB_COV = 1)#

Rather than scanning all points, this mode follows the event-driven BACnet standard, where only points with active BACnet subscriptions are published.

1. Execution Path

When #define BACNET_SUB_COV 1, the MQTT engine intercepts changes triggered during standard BACnet operations inside app_main.c:

  1. Received COV Event (Update_COV_Notify): Intercepted at line 2428 when a remote BACnet device notifies a change.
  2. Internal State Change (Update_Value_List): Intercepted at line 2522 when local points update, packaging the point's type, instance, value, and lifetime before calling the MQTT publish function.
C
#if BACNET_SUB_COV
    extern uint32_t Instance;
    cov_data.monitoredObjectIdentifier.type = type;
    cov_data.monitoredObjectIdentifier.instance = original_instance;
    cov_data.initiatingDeviceIdentifier = Instance;
    cov_data.subscriberProcessIdentifier = 1;
    cov_data.timeRemaining = 60;

    Mqtt_Handler_Send_COV(&cov_data);
#endif

2. Key Benefits

  • Bandwidth Efficiency: Drastically reduces network traffic since unsubscribed points do not generate MQTT payloads.
  • On-Demand Processing: CPU resources are only spent on serialization and publishing when a client actively monitors the point.

Mechanism C: MQTT-to-BACnet Subscription Forwarding Mode#

This mode allows clients on the MQTT broker to explicitly subscribe to any of the 6 point types (AI, AO, AV, BI, BO, BV) using JSON messages published to temco/test/tstat11/sub or temco/cov/tstat11/sub. The MQTT handler parses these requests and forwards them directly to the BACnet stack.

1. Execution Workflow

  1. Subscription JSON Received: The MQTT client receives a subscription/unsubscription JSON message on temco/test/tstat11/sub or temco/cov/tstat11/sub.
  2. JSON Parsing: The handler extracts the action ("subscribe" or "unsubscribe"), object_type, instance, and lifetime fields.
  3. Forwarding to BACnet: In mqtt_forward_subscription_to_bacnet(), the handler encodes a standard BACnet Subscribe COV request APDU:
    C
    cov_data.subscriberProcessIdentifier = 1; // MQTT process identifier
cov_data.monitoredObjectIdentifier.type = object_type;
cov_data.monitoredObjectIdentifier.instance = instance;
cov_data.issueConfirmedNotifications = false;
cov_data.lifetime = lifetime;
cov_data.cancellationRequest = is_unsubscribe;
  4. Local Stack Registration: It invokes handler_cov_subscribe() locally. The BACnet stack registers this subscription in its internal COV subscription table (COV_Subscriptions), bypassing any network transmission logic and directly monitoring the target point.
  5. Event Dispatch: When the point's value changes, the BACnet stack triggers a change notification which is intercepted in Update_Value_List or Update_COV_Notify, automatically calling Mqtt_Handler_Send_COV() to publish the update to the broker.

2. Key Benefits

  • Unified Stack Integration: Bypasses the need for duplicate subscription tables, polling tasks, or custom flash storage (NVS) implementations in the MQTT handler.
  • 100% Native Compatibility: Native BACnet deadbands, lifetimes, and object types are leveraged automatically.
  • Low Memory Footprint: The subscription is managed inside the existing BACnet COV database, requiring 0 extra bytes of RAM inside the MQTT handler component.

5. JSON Serialization and Type Mapping#

Mqtt_Handler_Send_COV translates structured C structures into a nested JSON schema using cJSON.

Data Type Translation Matrix#

The BACnet application tag type is evaluated and converted into native JSON types:

BACnet Tag Constants C Data Type JSON Output Representation
BACNET_APPLICATION_TAG_NULL N/A null
BACNET_APPLICATION_TAG_BOOLEAN bool true or false
BACNET_APPLICATION_TAG_UNSIGNED_INT uint32_t Number
BACNET_APPLICATION_TAG_SIGNED_INT int32_t Number
BACNET_APPLICATION_TAG_REAL float Number (Float)
BACNET_APPLICATION_TAG_DOUBLE double Number (Double)
BACNET_APPLICATION_TAG_ENUMERATED uint32_t Number
BACNET_APPLICATION_TAG_CHARACTER_STRING char[] String
BACNET_APPLICATION_TAG_OBJECT_ID BACNET_OBJECT_ID Object: {"type": <num>, "instance": <num>}
Others (Unsupported) N/A String: "(unsupported_tag)"

Topic Generation Logic#

The topic is constructed dynamically using the mapped display_instance to prevent namespaces from colliding on public brokers:

C
char topic[128];
snprintf(topic, sizeof(topic), "temco/cov/tstat11/device_%lu/%s_%lu",
         cov_data->initiatingDeviceIdentifier,
         bactext_object_type_name(cov_data->monitoredObjectIdentifier.type),
         display_instance);
  • Resulting topic: temco/cov/tstat11/device_<device_id>/<object_type_name>_<display_instance>

6. Debugging and Diagnostics#

To inspect the MQTT client operations and troubleshoot point subscription flows, the component contains built-in debug logging.

A. Enabling Debug Prints#

Set the preprocessor flag MQTT_DEBUG_EN to 1 at the top of Mqtt_Handler.c:

C
#define MQTT_DEBUG_EN 1

B. Debug Log Structure#

When enabled, debug logs are output via ESP-IDF's logging system under the tag MQTT_HANDLER prefixed with [DEBUG]. The logs cover:

  1. Command Reception: Logs the exact incoming topic and payload. Received topic: temco/cov/tstat11/sub, payload: {"action":"subscribe","object_type":"ANALOG_INPUT","instance":1,"lifetime":300}
  2. BACnet Forwarding: Logs when the parsed MQTT subscription is successfully encoded and forwarded to the BACnet stack. Forwarding subscription to BACnet: type=0, instance=1, lifetime=300, unsubscribe=0
  3. Dispatch Outcomes: Reports success or failure for the MQTT publish (Mqtt_Handler_Send_COV). Publishing COV to topic: temco/cov/tstat11/device_1028/Analog Input_1 COV MQTT message queued successfully, msg_id=47021

firmware/what-the-firmware-runs.title: What the firmware runs
firmware/what-the-firmware-runs.html:
The same firmware image runs on several Temco products. This page is the product list, because a behaviour that looks wrong on one model is often correct on another: the model id decides the IO envelope, the protocol surface and whether there is a display at all.

This project implements the core firmware used in TEMCO programmable HVAC and building automation controllers.

It provides Ethernet, WiFi, and RS485 connectivity, and exposes sensors, I/O, and control logic through standard Modbus and Bacnet protocols. Devices running this firmware can be accessed by third-party systems via Modbus and Bacnet, or automatically scanned, configured, and monitored using TEMCO’s T3000 software.

The same codebase is shared across multiple TEMCO products to provide a consistent, fully programmable building automation platform.

Products Using This Project#

T3 Series Programmable Bacnet & Modbus Controller#

The T3 controllers and Tstat10 are general-purpose programmable HVAC and building automation controllers.

This project provides its core communication, networking, and protocol handling, enabling multi-protocol operation (Modbus RTU/IP and Bacnet MSTP/IP) over Ethernet, WiFi, and RS485, with support for expandable I/O and advanced control logic via T3000.

Highlights

  • Programmable HVAC and building automation controller
  • Ethernet, WiFi, RS485 connectivity supported by this firmware
  • Modbus RTU / IP and Bacnet MSTP / IP protocol support
  • Expandable I/O architecture for scalable systems
  • Discovered, configured, and maintained using T3000 software
  • No licenses or recurring cloud fees

TSTAT10 Fully Programmable Thermostat#

TSTAT10 is a programmable thermostat and room controller with a local color LCD display and universal I/O.

This project enables its ESP32 networking stack, RS485 communication, and protocol integration, allowing the device to operate as part of a larger building automation system while remaining configurable through T3000 or direct register access.

Highlights

  • Fully programmable thermostat and room controller
  • Universal I/O configurable by software
  • RS485 communication with Modbus and Bacnet support
  • Local color LCD display with real-time data visualization
  • Well-documented register map for esay integration
  • Seamless integration with T3000 software

hardware/flash-layout.title: How flash is divided
hardware/flash-layout.html:
The flash layout is a device-safety contract between the first-stage bootloader, the TEMCO boot/update application, and the normal controller application.

Installed/recovery package layout#

The approved T3-S latest recovery package contains a partition-table.bin that decodes as follows:

Name Type Subtype Offset Size What normally occupies it
nvs data nvs 0x9000 0x10000 Controller settings
otadata data ota 0x19000 0x2000 Selects factory/OTA application state
phy_init data phy 0x1B000 0x1000 PHY calibration data
factory app factory 0x20000 0x100000 T3_bootloader.bin
ota_0 app ota_0 0x120000 0x600000 temco_app.bin after T3000 update
matter data nvs 0x720000 0x40000 Matter data
storage data nvs 0x760000 0x20000 Storage
screen_data data spiffs 0x780000 0x100000 Screen resources

The matching four-file UART flash map is:

File Address
bootloader.bin 0x0
partition-table.bin 0x8000
ota_data_initial.bin 0x19000
T3_bootloader.bin 0x20000

This makes the two application binaries intentionally different:

  • T3_bootloader.bin is the approximately 1 MB TEMCO update application in the factory partition.
  • temco_app.bin is the larger normal controller application loaded into the 6 MB OTA partition by T3000.

Where the package's ota_data_initial.bin comes from#

otadata is the partition the ESP-IDF second-stage bootloader reads to decide which application to start. ota_data_initial.bin is that partition's initial content — 8192 bytes with no selection recorded, so the factory application runs first.

Both projects generate one because both partition tables declare otadata at 0x19000. In the packages examined here the two files are byte-identical, so either copy is the same content. It is flashed at 0x19000 in the full-reflash flow, and it is not a firmware image that T3000 would select.

Application-project layout warning#

The current T3-programmable-controller-on-ESP32 checkout has a different temco_partitions.csv: its factory partition is 6 MB and ota_0 is 1 MB at 0x620000. That does not describe the decoded latest recovery package above.

The package's layout is the temco_partitions.csv from the bootloader branch Bhavik_Tstate11. That branch is the ESP32-S3 one; the bootloader repository's main is the older ESP32 / 4 MB variant.

Do not mix the application project's generated partition-table.bin with the recovery package's bootloader.bin, T3_bootloader.bin and OTA data. A ~2.7 MB temco_app.bin cannot fit the application project's 1 MB ota_0, so that mix fails at update time even though the flash tool reports success.

The bootloader and all application data must agree on the exact partition names, offsets and sizes. Use build\flasher_args.json or build\flash_args for a specific application-project build, and the approved packaged address map above for the known recovery package.

hardware/model-matrix.title: The Tstat11 IO envelope
hardware/model-matrix.html:
The firmware decides how many points a model has from its model id, and MINI_TSTAT11 is id 29. The limits themselves come from the TSTAT10 set — main/commsub.c maps both ids onto TSTAT10_* — so a Tstat11 has the same envelope as a TSTAT10, and this table is the authoritative answer to "how many inputs does it have".

Model Model id AI DO AO AV DI SC
T3-BB (Big Brother) MINI_BIG_ARM = 5 32 12 12 128 0 8
T3-LB (Little Brother) MINI_SMALL_ARM = 6 16 6 4 128 0 8
T3-TB (Tiny Brother) MINI_NEW_TINY = 4 8 8 6 128 0 8
T3-Nano MINI_TINY_ARM = 7 11 6 2 128 0 8
VAV controller MINI_VAV = 10 6 1 2 5 0 8
TSTAT10 MINI_TSTAT10 = 9 13 5 2 128 8 8
T10P MINI_T10P = 11 17 5 4 128 8 8
Tstat11 MINI_TSTAT11 = 29 13 5 2 128 8 8

AI analog input · DO digital output · AO analog output · AV analog variable · DI digital input · SC schedule

What the columns are#

  • AI / DI — the input tables. A universal input counts in AI; the DI column is the fixed digital inputs some models add.
  • DO / AO — the output tables. DO is a relay or triac, AO is an analogue signal.
  • AV — the variable table, 128 on every model in this family, because variables are memory rather than terminals.
  • SC — schedules, eight on every model.

The Tstat11 row is the one to read: it is the TSTAT10 envelope, and the firmware special-cases the two ids together in six places in main/flash.c as well as in commsub.c.

t3-eez-studio/readme.title: Design Studio: how it is built
t3-eez-studio/readme.html:
Design Studio (Tstat11)#

Design Studio (Tstat11) is T3000's designer for embedded touchscreen UIs. You draw screens for the Tstat11 display, preview them in the browser, and deploy them to the controller — without writing firmware code.

You reach it from the Design Hub: open the Design Hub, pick an LVGL tile, and the editor opens.

Powered by EEZ Studio

The editor core — the LVGL project editor, the .eez-project file format, the EEZ Flow logic engine and the browser preview runtime — is integrated from the open-source EEZ Studio project (a free, cross-platform, GPL-3.0 tool for embedded GUIs, by Envox d.o.o.).

Because of this, the editor looks and behaves like EEZ Studio and uses the same vocabulary: pages, widgets, styles, variables and Flow. This manual documents the T3000 workflow around that core — the Design Hub, creating a project, binding a device and deploying — rather than re-teaching the editor itself.

Start here in 3 steps#

Step What you do
1. Pick a project type In the Design Hub, click the LVGL 9.5 tile (plain UI) or LVGL with Flow 9.5 (UI + logic).
2. Create the project Create New for a blank project, LVGL Examples to start from a ready-made design, or Load from Device to pull the screens already on a controller.
3. Design, preview, deploy Build your screens in the editor, preview with Run (F5), then Bind a device and click Deploy to Device.

The two project types#

Project type Choose it when you want…
LVGL 9.5 A touchscreen UI made of pages, widgets, styles, fonts and images.
LVGL with Flow 9.5 The same UI plus visual logic — a button that changes a value, a screen that reacts to data, animations and timers.

Both types produce an .eez-project file, preview in the browser and deploy to a device. Flow is a project setting, so it is not an irreversible choice.

Manual chapters#

# Chapter What's inside
01 Overview What Design Studio (Tstat11) is, the two project types, and a tour of every screen.
02 Creating a Project The three ways to start: Create New, from an Example, Load from Device.
03 Designing Screens The editor tour and how to build pages with widgets, styles, fonts and images.
04 Adding Logic with EEZ Flow Flow components, events, variables, and a worked example.
05 Preview, Bind & Deploy Preview in the browser, bind a controller, and deploy your design.
06 Reference & FAQ Feature matrix, routes, file locations, shortcuts, glossary and troubleshooting.

What you can do#

Capability LVGL 9.5 LVGL with Flow 9.5
Visual page/screen designer Yes Yes
Widget library (label, button, switch, slider, bar, image, panel…) Yes Yes
Styles, themes, fonts Yes Yes
Bitmaps / images Yes Yes

Flow logic editor (actions, event handlers, timers) — Yes
Browser preview (Run mode) Yes Yes
Full simulator (F7) Yes Yes
Save / reopen project from disk Yes Yes
Bind to a device Yes Yes
Deploy to a device Yes Yes
Start from an EEZ example project Yes Yes
Load existing screens off a device Yes Yes

Related documentation#

Device-side logic — how the controller receives, stores and renders the screens, and the display REST API it exposes — is documented with the firmware:

  • DEVICE_REST_API_DISPLAY.md — firmware display REST API

Developer design docs for this feature live in this folder:

  • device-firmware-lvgl-architecture.md

t3-eez-studio/device-interface-deploymen.title: Deploying to a device
t3-eez-studio/device-interface-deploymen.html:
Deploy to Device — as built (REST)#

The REST implementation below is the current deployment path. The BACnet-based design this file originally described is kept at the end as an appendix.

Send a designed UI from the editor to a T3 controller, and load a controller's current screens back into the editor.

  • Deploy (push) — export the .eez-project, diff it against the last successful deploy, and push only what changed to the device.
  • Load from Device (pull) — read the device's screens and images into a new .eez-project. See import-from-device-design.md.
  • Save — .eez-project → device-native screen JSON. See lvgl-eez-project-json-format.md.

The user-facing walkthrough is in the manual: manual/05-preview-and-deploy.md.

The filename still says bacnet for link stability. The content is REST.

1. Transport#

Screens travel over HTTP REST through the T3000 host — not BACnet:

Text
Browser → /api/device-rest/<device-ip>/api/eez-device/<endpoint>
        → T3000 backend proxy → ESP32 HTTP server, port 80
Piece Where
Client src/lib/t3-eez-studio/project-editor/build/device-rest-client.ts
Base URL restUrl() → /api/device-rest/${deviceIp}/api/eez-device/${path}
Proxy T3000 backend — api/src/eez_studio/mod.rs → proxy_device_rest (the device sends no CORS headers, so the browser cannot call it directly)
Deploy timeout DEPLOY_TIMEOUT_MS = 120000 for push operations; 30 s for reads
Device server firmware components/temco_dynamic_display (esp_http_server, port 80)
Device storage SPIFFS partition screen_data → /spiffs/screens/<name>.json

DeviceRestClient is REST-only. The BACnet fallback from the original design was dropped — the fallback code paths in device-rest-client.ts are commented out, and USE_MOCK = false.

connect(ip, panelId, serialNumber) probes GET device/info and returns { mode: "rest", deviceIp }, or an error when the device is unreachable. Timeouts: 10 s reachability, 30 s request, 120 s deploy.

The client's own docstring still says it talks "straight to the device" — that comment is stale; every request goes through the T3000 proxy path above.

2. Endpoint contract#

Device endpoints (all under /api/eez-device):

Method Endpoint Purpose
GET /device/info Screen list + counts. screens is an object keyed screen1..N, not an array
GET /screens All screens
GET /screens/:name One screen
PUT /screens Deploy all — body { screens: [{ name, json }] }
PUT /screens/:name Deploy one — body { json }
PATCH /screens/:name Dot-path delta — body { changes: [{ path, value }] }
POST /images/push Upload image — body { name, data_base64 }
GET /images/pull/:name Download image
DELETE /images/:name Remove image
POST /reset-defaults, /set-default-screens, /load-default-screens Default-screen management

Limits and gaps (as implemented):

  • Request bodies are capped at 512 KB; exceeding it returns 400 (not 413).
  • device/info reports serial_number: 0, firmware_version: "1.0.0" and lvgl_version: "9.1.0" as hard-coded literals — they are not read from the panel.
  • Images are stored as the raw request body text (base64 inside JSON), not decoded pixels.
  • There is no delete-screen endpoint — only images can be deleted.

Legacy BACnet-style aliases exist on the device (POST /screens/push/:panelId, POST /screens/pull/:panelId) but the client does not use them.

3. Deploy pipeline (incremental)#

src/t3-react/features/design-hub/services/deployService.ts → deployEezProject() is the single deploy implementation. Both the editor toolbar (Deploy to Device) and the Design Hub drawer call it.

# Step Notes
1 save Editor path only — persist the in-memory project first
2 load Read .eez-project from disk via GET /api/eez-studio/read-text-file
3 export transformToDeviceJson() → one device screen per page; extractDeviceImages() → bitmaps
4 backup Write device-export/<Screen>.json (minified) + device-export/images/<name>.png
5 diff Compare against device-export/deploy-manifest.json
6 bind setDeviceBinding(filePath, { ip, panelId, serialNumber, … })
7 push Changed images (POST images/push), then changed screens (PUT /screens/:name). A full deploy calls deployAllScreens() → PUT /screens
8 manifest Rewrite deploy-manifest.json only after a fully successful push
9 log Append to the deploy log and mark the project Deployed

Change detection#

  • MANIFEST_HASH_VERSION = 2, stored in deploy-manifest.json.
  • Screens use canonicalSignature() (project-editor/build/deploy-manifest.ts) — order-insensitive, so a re-export that only reorders keys is not a change.
  • Images use contentSignature().
  • First deploy / no usable manifest: the baseline falls back to what the device returned during Load from Device — device-import/<screen>.json and device-import/imgs/<name>.png. That is the authoritative "what the device already had" snapshot, so an unchanged re-export is not pushed back.
  • Nothing changed → the push step reports skipped.
  • A failed push does not update the manifest, so the next deploy retries the remainder.

4. Entry points#

Entry point File
Editor toolbar → Deploy to Device src/lib/t3-eez-studio/project-editor/project/ui/Toolbar.tsx
Design Hub drawer / project detail src/t3-react/features/design-hub/components/DeployDeviceDrawer.tsx
Device lookup (both) fetchDeployDevices() → GET http://<host>:9103/api/t3_device/devices

Port 9103 is the T3000 host backend, not the device. It is only used to list devices; the push itself goes through /api/device-rest/<ip>/….

Appendix — Original BACnet design#

Historical. Everything below describes an earlier BACnet deployment proposal rather than the shipped pipeline: deployment goes over REST (1. Transport through 4. Entry points above), there is no POST /api/devices/:id/deploy-firmware, and WEBVIEW_MESSAGE_TYPE has no Action 18. The BACnet transfer details (200-byte chunks, zlib) belong to that proposal.

The BACnet Private Data commands the firmware implements are WRITE_JSON_SCREEN = 186 / WRITE_JSON_ITEM = 187 (read 86 / 87) in temco_bacnet/private/ptransfer.c; they copy into fixed slots of 50 bytes (screen) and 200 bytes (item), uncompressed. See ../bacnet-api/commands.md.

1. Current State#

firmware-export.ts transforms .eez-project → per-screen firmware JSON files (one per screen, ~30KB each). "Deploy" button writes files to disk — does not reach hardware. See EEZ Project JSON Format.

The T3000 already pushes graphic data to devices over BACnet. Firmware deploy can reuse the same path:

Existing pipe: Browser → HTTP → Rust → FFI → C++ → BACnet → Device

  • write_webview_data() in BacnetScreen.cpp:164 reads a zip file, chunks it into 200-byte blocks, and pushes it to the device via WritePrivateData_Blocking.
  • WEBVIEW_MESSAGE_TYPE in BacnetWebView.cpp:61 defines actions 0–17 — Rust has the same enum in t3_ffi_sync_service.rs:53.
  • call_handle_webview_msg() in t3_ffi_sync_service.rs:246 is the Rust → C++ bridge, calling BacnetWebView_HandleWebViewMsg() in BacnetWebView_Exports.cpp:97 which dispatches to the handler.

2. Recommended Approach#

Extend the existing WEBVIEW_MESSAGE_TYPE enum with a new action (18) and reuse the same 200-byte chunked WritePrivateData_Blocking pattern from SAVE_GRAPHIC_DATA (action 2).

2.1. Send Firmware to Device#

Layer Change
Rust + C++ enum Add DEPLOY_FIRMWARE = 18 to WebViewMessageType in t3_ffi_sync_service.rs:53 and BacnetWebView.cpp:61
Rust route New POST /api/devices/:id/deploy-firmware — wraps firmware JSON with action=18, calls call_handle_webview_msg()
C++ handler New case DEPLOY_FIRMWARE in HandleWebViewMsg() — compresses JSON, chunks 200B blocks, pushes via WritePrivateData_Blocking(WRITE_JSON_ITEM)
Browser Wire "Deploy" button in Toolbar.tsx to the new endpoint

2.1.1. Architecture

Text
┌──────────┐  HTTP POST      ┌──────────┐  FFI (DLL export)   ┌──────────┐  BACnet chunks  ┌──────────┐
│ Browser  │ ──────────────→ │  Rust    │ ─────────────────→  │  C++     │ ──────────────→ │  Device  │
│ (EEZ)    │ ←────────────── │  (api/)  │ ←─────────────────  │ (T3000)  │ ←────────────── │ (HW)     │
└──────────┘    JSON         └──────────┘   in-place buffer   └──────────┘  200B blocks    └──────────┘
                                │                                    │
                      call_handle_webview_msg()           WritePrivateData_Blocking()
                      t3_ffi_sync_service.rs:246          WRITE_JSON_SCREEN + WRITE_JSON_ITEM

Why this path? The T3000 already has SAVE_GRAPHIC_DATA (action=2) doing exactly this — receiving graphic JSON from browser, writing to disk, zipping, chunking into 200-byte blocks, and pushing to device via WritePrivateData_Blocking. Firmware deploy is the same pattern: we skip the disk step and send firmware JSON directly through the Rust→C++ bridge.

2.1.2. New WEBVIEW_MESSAGE_TYPE Enum Extension

Both enums must stay in sync. Add to:

Rust — api/src/t3_device/t3_ffi_sync_service.rs:53:

RUST
pub enum WebViewMessageType {
    // ... existing 0-17 ...
    DEPLOY_FIRMWARE = 18,  // ← NEW: deploy firmware screen JSON to device
}

C++ — T3000/BacnetWebView.cpp:61:

C++
enum WEBVIEW_MESSAGE_TYPE {
    // ... existing 0-17 ...
